title: Common mistakes that sink design rounds
scopeHtml: Scope: eight frequent mistakes and how to fix them.

notes.title: Mistake 1: designing before clarifying
notes.html:
The most common failure is solving a problem nobody asked. Without scope, you build chat with video calls, search, payments and end-to-end encryption, then run out of time with nothing deep.

Fix: spend the first 3 to 5 minutes on 3 to 5 sharp questions, then repeat the scope back: "so we support 1:1 and group text, delivery receipts, no media, 50M DAU, correct?"

Worked example. "Design YouTube" can mean upload and transcoding, playback streaming, search, recommendations or comments. Each is a different system. If you pick "upload plus playback, 100M DAU, no recommendations", you can reach real depth (transcoding pipeline, CDN) in 45 minutes.

Industry examples. Real design docs at Google and Amazon list "non-goals" explicitly for the same reason; unbounded scope kills projects.

Decision gravity. Scope is reversible in the room (the interviewer can widen it) but each added feature adds boxes, so be deliberate.

Everyday analogy. Ordering food: "what do you feel like?" before the waiter starts cooking.

Common interview traps.

  • Asking 15 questions with no effect on the design.
  • Never stating assumptions, so the interviewer cannot correct you early.

notes.title: Mistake 2: no numbers
notes.html:
A design without numbers cannot be judged. "We'll use a cache" is meaningless without how big, how many requests, what hit ratio.

Fix: do the estimation (see F3), and attach a number to every major decision: cache size, shard count, partition count, replica count, TTL.

Worked example. "Peak 70K reads/s; cache absorbs 95%, leaving 3.5K reads/s for Postgres, one primary and two replicas are enough. 200 writes/s fits one primary. So no sharding yet." That one paragraph shows you can be trusted with capacity decisions.

Industry examples. Capacity reviews at Netflix, Uber and Stripe start from QPS, latency percentile and storage growth; numbers are the common language between teams.

Everyday analogy. A recipe without quantities.

Common interview traps.

  • Numbers at the start, then forgotten when choosing components.
  • Wildly wrong orders of magnitude (off by 1000x) that go unnoticed.

notes.title: Mistake 3: buzzword stacking and over-engineering
notes.html:
Kafka, Redis, Cassandra, Kubernetes, microservices, all by minute five. More boxes means more failure modes and more cost. Senior engineers are valued for choosing the simplest design that meets the numbers.

Fix: start with a monolith-ish stateless tier plus a relational DB. Add a component only when a requirement or number demands it, and say which one.

Worked example. 200 writes/s and 5 TB of data: a single Postgres with replicas handles it. Proposing Cassandra plus Kafka plus Elasticsearch adds three systems to run for no gain. At 200K writes/s, 500 TB, the story changes.

Industry examples. Stack Overflow ran on a few SQL Server machines; Instagram's early stack was Django, Postgres, Redis, memcached. Shopify scaled a Rails monolith for years with sharded MySQL (pods). Segment and Amazon Prime Video have publicly written about moving from microservices back to a monolith for cost and simplicity.

Decision gravity. Microservices are a near one-way door: splitting is easy, merging back is painful and distributed transactions cost you consistency. Start modular and split on team or scaling pressure.

Everyday analogy. Buying a truck to carry a loaf of bread.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming a technology without saying what it replaces or why.
  • Choosing a NoSQL database "for scale" when the data is relational and small.

notes.title: Mistake 4: ignoring failure and edge cases
notes.html:
Designs that assume everything works are mid-level. The senior signal is to describe what happens when it does not: node crash, network partition, duplicate message, retry storm, slow dependency, hot key.

Fix: for each component ask four questions: what if it is down, slow, wrong, or overloaded? Mention timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, idempotency keys, circuit breakers, dead-letter queues.

Worked example. Payment call times out. Did it succeed? Retrying could double-charge. Answer: client sends an idempotency key, server stores key and result for 24 h; a retry with the same key returns the stored result. Stripe's API works exactly this way.

Industry examples. AWS's 2017 S3 outage (a typo in a command removed too many servers) and Facebook's October 2021 BGP outage are standard case studies in cascading failure and missing safeguards. Netflix uses Hystrix-style circuit breakers and chaos testing.

Production symptom. Retry storm: dependency slows, clients retry, load triples, dependency dies. The metric to watch is request rate versus success rate; with retries, request rate climbs while successes fall.

Everyday analogy. Wearing a seatbelt: you do not expect to crash, you plan for it.

Common interview traps.

  • Retries without backoff, jitter or a cap.
  • Exactly-once claims; real systems do at-least-once plus idempotent handling.
  • Forgetting the load balancer, queue or cache as single points of failure.

notes.title: Mistake 5: ignoring trade-offs and consistency
notes.html:
Every choice gives something up. Saying "it has no downside" is a red flag. The classic ones: consistency vs availability, latency vs durability, cost vs speed, read vs write optimisation, simplicity vs flexibility.

Fix: use a template for each decision: "I choose X because Y; the alternative is Z, which is better when W; X breaks when V."

Worked example. Cache plus DB. Write-through keeps cache fresh but doubles write latency (say 2 ms to 5 ms); cache-aside (invalidate on write) is simpler but allows a stale read for a few milliseconds after a race. For a profile page the stale read is fine; for an account balance it is not, so read balance from the primary.

Industry examples. Amazon's Dynamo chose availability and eventual consistency for the shopping cart; Google Spanner pays commit latency (TrueTime waits, on the order of several milliseconds) to give external consistency. Both were deliberate.

Decision gravity. Consistency model is usually a one-way door because application code assumes it; weakening later breaks invariants, strengthening later costs latency and a migration.

Everyday analogy. Fast, cheap, good: pick two.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming strong consistency and high availability across partitions (CAP).
  • Not saying which data needs which consistency level.

notes.title: Mistake 6: poor communication and rigid behaviour
notes.html:
Silence, monologue, defensiveness and ignoring hints sink strong engineers. The interviewer is a collaborator who wants to see how you work in a team.

Fixes:

  • Think aloud in short sentences; summarise your plan before each phase.
  • Check in: "does this direction work, or should I go deeper elsewhere?"
  • Treat hints as free gifts: "good point, that changes X, let me revise."
  • Use the whiteboard tidily: left to right data flow, label arrows, number the steps.

Worked example. Interviewer: "what if one user has 50M followers?" Weak: "that won't happen." Strong: "that breaks fan-out on write, since a post costs 50M writes. I would switch celebrities to fan-out on read and merge at read time. Thanks, that also affects the cache size."

Industry examples. Hiring rubrics at large companies score collaboration separately (often called communication or "working with the interviewer") because design work in real life is a team activity: design reviews, RFCs, incident calls.

Everyday analogy. Pair driving: the navigator helps; arguing about the route wastes time.

Common interview traps.

  • Arguing with feedback instead of exploring it.
  • Reading from a memorised script and not noticing the interviewer is lost.
  • Not handling a mistake gracefully; admit, fix, move on.

notes.title: Mistake 7: shallow breadth, no depth; and bad time use
notes.html:
Ten boxes and no deep dive is the classic mid-level pattern. Seniors pick a hard part and go to mechanism: data structures, protocols, failure behaviour, numbers.

Fix: after the high-level design, say "I will go deep on X because it is the riskiest part". Know at least five deep topics well: sharding and rebalancing, replication and failover, caching and invalidation, queues and delivery semantics, consistency and transactions.

Worked example. Deep dive on "sharding the messages table": choose key (conversation_id, not user_id, so one chat lives on one shard), 64 logical shards on 8 physical nodes (so you can rebalance without re-hashing), hot conversation handling, cross-shard queries via a separate index. That is a full senior answer.

Industry examples. Instagram used logical shards mapped onto fewer physical Postgres servers; Pinterest sharded MySQL with a mapping table; Slack's Vitess adoption is a modern example of operating sharding at scale.

Time use. Over-long estimation or API sections starve the deep dive; keep to the timeline from F1 and say when you are skipping something on purpose.

Everyday analogy. A doctor who orders every test but diagnoses nothing.

Common interview traps.

  • Mentioning sharding but unable to say what the shard key is, or what breaks (cross-shard joins, hot shard).
  • Running out of time before covering failure and monitoring.
  • Treating the interviewer's deep question as an attack rather than an invitation.

notes.title: Mistake 8: forgetting operations, security and cost
notes.html:
Real systems must be run. Candidates who never mention monitoring, deployment, rate limiting, authentication, data privacy or cost look like they have never been on call.

Mention briefly:

  • Observability: p50/p99 latency, error rate, saturation (queue lag, connection pool), tracing IDs.
  • Rollout: canary or blue-green, feature flags, backward-compatible schema changes.
  • Security: authN/authZ, TLS, rate limiting, input validation, PII encryption.
  • Cost: biggest line (egress, storage, compute) and one lever to cut it.

Worked example. "Alert if p99 > 500 ms for 5 minutes or error rate > 1%; deploy 5% canary for 15 minutes; rate limit 100 req/min per user at the gateway; move media older than 90 days to cold storage to cut the largest cost line by roughly 60%." Concrete, short, believable.

Industry examples. Google's SRE golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) are a standard checklist. Stripe, Cloudflare and AWS publish public post-mortems that show how missing rollouts safeguards cause incidents.

Decision gravity. Observability and rollout are cheap to add early and expensive to retrofit; schema-change discipline (expand then contract) is the difference between a safe migration and an outage.

Everyday analogy. A shop needs a till, locks and a cleaning schedule, not only shelves.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving security entirely out for a payments or health prompt.
  • Saying "we will monitor it" with no metric names.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Clarify scope first; state assumptions and non-goals.
  • Use numbers and let them drive every component choice.
  • Start simple; add components only when a number or requirement demands it.
  • Describe failure, retries, idempotency and single points of failure.
  • Name trade-offs for every decision, including consistency level and reversibility.
  • Communicate: think aloud, check in, take hints gracefully.
  • Go deep on the riskiest part; manage time; finish with operations, security and cost.

questions.promptHtml: You get "Design YouTube." What do you do in the first five minutes and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Unbounded prompts are deliberate. The signal is whether you scope before building.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask 3 to 5 sharp questions, then repeat the scope back: which features (upload and playback, not recommendations), scale (say 100M DAU), and constraints (latency, regions). Then I state non-goals. That lets me go deep on transcoding and CDN instead of drawing ten shallow boxes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
"YouTube" can mean upload and transcoding, streaming, search, recommendations or comments, each a different system. Good questions change the design: read:write ratio, peak shape, file sizes, consistency needs, global or one region. Bad questions (15 of them, with no effect on the design) waste time.

Prompt -> 3-5 questions -> confirm scope + assumptions -> design

Real design docs list non-goals for the same reason. Scope is reversible in the room; the interviewer can widen it, but each feature adds boxes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Asking many questions with no design effect.
  • Not stating assumptions so they cannot be corrected.
  • Treating the prompt as a memorised template.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if they say "you decide"? -> State assumptions and numbers, ask them to veto.
  2. Which question matters most? -> The one that changes the architecture: scale, read:write, consistency.
  3. When do you stop clarifying? -> When the next answer would not change a component or a number.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE jumps to boxes. Senior scopes, states non-goals and assumptions, and sets the depth plan.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Project RFCs with no non-goals expand until the date slips.

questions.promptHtml: Why are numbers essential in a design round, and how do you tie them to decisions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "We'll use a cache" is unfalsifiable. Numbers show you can be trusted with capacity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every major decision gets a number: peak QPS, hit ratio, shard count, TTL, replica count. For example, 70K peak reads, 95% cache hit leaves 3.5K reads for Postgres, one primary and two replicas, 200 writes/s fits one primary, so no sharding yet.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Peak 70K QPS -> hit 95% -> DB 3.5K QPS -> 1 primary + 2 replicas

The pattern: estimate load (see estimation topic), pick component, check against its per-node capacity, then say what number would make you change it. Numbers also expose being off by 1000x, which is the commonest embarrassing error.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Numbers at the start, forgotten when choosing components.
  • Order-of-magnitude errors unnoticed (average vs peak, bits vs bytes).
  • False precision.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you handle unknown numbers? -> Assume, state, and show sensitivity ("if 10x, then...").
  2. What numbers do you always get? -> Peak QPS, read:write, data size per day, latency target.
  3. How do you present them? -> One line per decision on the board.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE states an estimate once. Senior ties each component to a number and names the trigger to change it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Capacity reviews start from QPS, percentile latency and storage growth, which makes numbers the shared language.

questions.promptHtml: How do you present a design decision so it shows trade-off awareness? Use cache write strategies as the example.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "No downside" is a red flag; interviewers listen for structure and for the consistency choice per data type.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I choose X because Y; the alternative Z is better when W; X breaks when V." For caching: write-through keeps the cache fresh but raises write latency (about 2 ms to 5 ms); cache-aside with invalidation is simpler but allows a brief stale read after a race. A profile page tolerates that; an account balance reads from the primary.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Common axes: consistency vs availability, latency vs durability, cost vs speed, read vs write optimisation, simplicity vs flexibility. Decision gravity: consistency model is usually a one-way door because application code assumes it; weakening later breaks invariants, strengthening costs latency and migration. Examples: Dynamo chose availability for the cart; Spanner pays commit latency for external consistency. Both deliberate.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming strong consistency and full availability across partitions.
  • One consistency level for every kind of data.
  • No mention of reversibility.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where would you demand strong consistency? -> Money, inventory counts, uniqueness constraints.
  2. Where is eventual fine? -> Feeds, counters for display, profiles.
  3. How do you move from eventual to strong later? -> Costly; needs data migration and write-path changes, so decide early.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE picks a pattern. Senior states why, what it costs, when it breaks, and per data type.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team using cache-aside for balances showed customers wrong funds after a race, and had to add primary reads.

questions.promptHtml: After the high-level design, how do you choose and run a deep dive, and how do you manage time?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Ten boxes and no depth is the classic mid-level pattern.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I say "I will go deep on X because it is the riskiest part", then cover mechanism, numbers and failure: for a chat app, sharding the messages table by conversation_id, 64 logical shards on 8 physical nodes, hot conversations, cross-shard queries via an index. I keep estimation and API sections short and say when I skip something on purpose.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
boxes -> riskiest part -> mechanism -> numbers -> failure -> monitoring

Have five deep topics ready: sharding and rebalancing, replication and failover, caching and invalidation, queues and delivery semantics, consistency and transactions. Logical shards decouple key placement from node count so you rebalance without re-hashing. Time: follow the timeline; do not let estimation eat the deep dive.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mentioning sharding without a shard key or what breaks.
  • Running out of time before failure and monitoring.
  • Treating a deep question as an attack.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why conversation_id and not user_id? -> One chat lives on one shard so reads are single-shard.
  2. What about a hot key? -> Split or cache, see hot-key handling.
  3. How do you rebalance? -> Move logical shards between nodes with dual-write then cutover.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists components. Senior picks the risk, goes to mechanism and quantifies.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Instagram-style logical shards mapped to fewer physical nodes allowed growth without re-keying.

questions.contextHtml: A candidate is designing an internal order system: 200 writes per second at peak, 5 TB of data, 2,000 reads per second, 10 engineers. By minute 5 the candidate has drawn microservices, Kafka, Cassandra, Elasticsearch and Kubernetes. The interviewer asks: "Why Cassandra here?" The answer is "for scale."
questions.promptHtml: Critique this and show the design you would present.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Defends the stack or lists features of each tool.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Growth over 2 to 3 years? Consistency needs (orders are transactional)? Query patterns? Team ops skills?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reset: "Let me simplify using the numbers."
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 200 writes/s and 2K reads/s fit one Postgres primary with replicas (capacity roughly 1K to 10K writes/s); the data is relational; each extra system adds failure modes and cost.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare numbers to per-node capacity; list what each added component would fix. None does.
  5. Root cause: Technology chosen before requirements.
  6. Fix: A modular monolith or few services, Postgres with 2 replicas, Redis only if hit-ratio math demands, search added when a real search requirement arrives. Say the triggers: writes above ~5K/s, data over ~20 TB, or a second team.
  7. Prevention: Each component needs a one-line justification from a number.
  8. Trade-offs: Microservices are near one-way; splitting is easy and merging back is painful, so stay modular and split on team or scaling pressure. Public examples (a few companies moved services back to a monolith for cost) support this.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Writes become 200K/s? -> Then partitioned or distributed stores and queues earn their place.
  • Full-text search needed? -> Add a search index fed from the DB; it is derived data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team ran three data stores for a table that fit in RAM; consolidating onto Postgres cut on-call pages in half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: defends buzzwords.
  • Hire: simplifies to numbers.
  • Strong hire: gives triggers for each addition and the reversibility of microservices.

questions.contextHtml: In a news-feed design, the candidate proposes fan-out on write for all users. Interviewer: "What if one user has 50M followers?" Candidate: "That would not happen." Interviewer: "It does. Think of a celebrity." Candidate says "we could just add more workers" and keeps talking for two minutes without pausing.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong with the communication, and how should the candidate have handled it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only fixes the technical answer, ignoring the behaviour.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (To myself) Is this a hint toward a known limit? What does 50M followers do to write cost?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop, thank the interviewer, and say "that breaks fan-out on write, one post costs 50M writes."
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Defensive reflex; monologue; ignoring the interviewer's signal.
  4. How I'd verify: Check back: "does this direction address your concern?"
  5. Root cause: Treating feedback as an attack instead of free information.
  6. Fix: Technical: hybrid. Fan-out on write for normal users, fan-out on read for celebrities, merge at read time; cache sizes change. Behavioural: think aloud in short sentences, summarise before each phase, check in.
  7. Prevention: Practise with mock interviews, note interruptions as hints.
  8. Trade-offs: The hybrid costs read-time merge complexity; adding workers fails because 50M writes per post at, say, 100K writes/s is 500 s of backlog per celebrity post.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer says it works? -> Still state the limit you would monitor.
  • You made an error earlier? -> Admit, fix, move on.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A strong engineer lost an offer by arguing for ten minutes about a requirement the interviewer was clearly widening.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: denies and argues.
  • Hire: accepts and revises to the hybrid.
  • Strong hire: also quantifies the backlog and checks in.

questions.contextHtml:
In a payments design the candidate draws: client -> API -> payment provider -> DB. The interviewer asks: "The call to the provider times out after 10 seconds. What now?" The candidate says "retry it." Logs from a similar real system show:

12:00:01 POST /charge amount=49.00 user=77 -> timeout
12:00:11 POST /charge amount=49.00 user=77 -> 200 OK id=ch_1
12:00:12 provider webhook: charge ch_0 succeeded amount=49.00 user=77
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug in "just retry" and what is the correct design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a retry count or a longer timeout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the provider support idempotency keys? How long do we need to dedupe? Is the user-facing flow sync?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop blind retries; check status via lookup before any new charge; refund duplicates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The first request succeeded at the provider but the response was lost, so the retry created a second charge (ch_0 and ch_1 for the same order).
  4. How I'd verify: Reconcile provider records against order IDs.
  5. Root cause: A timeout means unknown outcome, not failure.
  6. Fix: Client generates an idempotency key (per order attempt); server stores key and result for 24 h; a retry with the same key returns the stored result; provider call includes the key. Add reconciliation job and a pending state.
  7. Prevention: Backoff with jitter and a retry cap; alert on duplicate charges.
  8. Trade-offs: Exactly-once is not available; I design at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handling. Key storage costs a little space and a lookup per request.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two retries race in parallel? -> Unique constraint on the key; second waits or gets conflict.
  • Key reused with a different amount? -> Reject with an error.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A double-charge incident came from a gateway retry that nobody on the service team knew about; the fix was keys end to end.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries blindly.
  • Hire: idempotency key and stored result.
  • Strong hire: unknown-outcome reasoning, reconciliation, race handling.

questions.contextHtml:
A downstream inventory service had a 2-minute slowdown. Dashboards at 10:14:

             10:10    10:12    10:14
inv p99      90ms     4.8s     timeouts
client rps   2,000    6,100    9,800
success rps  2,000    1,300    300
inv cpu      45%      97%      100%
client retry config: 3 retries, no backoff, timeout 1s

The slowdown cause (a bad index deploy) was rolled back at 10:13, yet the service stays down until 10:25.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the outage outlast the cause, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the index and calls it resolved at rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do clients share a library? Is there a circuit breaker? Are other services calling inventory?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load: block or rate limit retries at the gateway; reduce client traffic to let inventory drain; scale only after load is controlled.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Retry amplification: up to 4 attempts per request, so rps climbed 5x while success fell; queues full of stale work; the red herring is the rollback, which worked.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare request rate to success rate (rising vs falling), queue depth, retry headers.
  5. Root cause: Metastable failure: retries sustain overload even after the trigger is gone.
  6. Fix: Exponential backoff with jitter and a cap, retry budget (e.g. retries at most 10% of requests), circuit breakers, timeouts shorter than caller deadlines, server-side load shedding.
  7. Prevention: Alert when request rate rises while success rate falls; chaos test slow dependencies.
  8. Trade-offs: Circuit breakers fail fast and cost some availability during partial recovery; I would not just add replicas because they would also be overwhelmed by the retry multiplier.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retries in three layers? -> Multiply: 4 x 4 x 4 = 64; retry at one layer only.
  • Non-idempotent calls? -> Do not retry without keys.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 90 second blip turned into 40 minutes because three libraries each retried three times.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames root trigger only.
  • Hire: identifies retry amplification and fixes backoff.
  • Strong hire: retry budgets, layered multiplication, load shedding, metastability.

questions.contextHtml: A 45-minute round for "design a ride-hailing backend". Minute log of a candidate: 0-12 requirements and detailed estimation (7 numbers, 3 conversions), 12-20 API for 14 endpoints, 20-30 high-level diagram with 11 boxes, 30-40 data model, 40-45 "what about scaling?" The interviewer wrote: "good fundamentals, never saw the hard part: matching drivers by location."
questions.promptHtml: Re-plan the 45 minutes and explain what you would deliberately skip.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Be faster at everything."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which part does the interviewer care about? (Ask at minute 10.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: If late, say "I will skip the remaining endpoints and go deep on matching."
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Time spent on low-signal sections; no explicit depth choice; deep topics unprepared.
  4. How I'd verify: Plan with checkpoints: 5 min scope, 5 estimates, 5 API (3 key endpoints), 8 high-level, 15 deep dive, 5 failure/ops/cost.
  5. Root cause: Treating all sections as equal.
  6. Fix: Deep dive: geospatial index (geohash or H3 cells), driver locations updated every 4 seconds from 1M drivers is 250K updates/s held in memory sharded by cell; matching within a cell and neighbours; surge on hot cells; failure when a shard dies.
  7. Prevention: Practise with a timer, rehearse five deep-dive topics.
  8. Trade-offs: Skipping detailed estimation risks missing scale, so do one-line numbers; skipping all 14 endpoints is fine if stated.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer asks for the data model after all? -> Give it briefly, then return.
  • A hot downtown cell? -> Smaller cells or finer sharding for dense areas.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Candidates who announced "I will skip X on purpose" scored higher than those who ran out of time silently.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: equal time on everything, no depth.
  • Hire: names and executes a deep dive.
  • Strong hire: explicit time plan, numbers in the deep dive, deliberate skips.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet app uses cache-aside on Redis (TTL 60 s) over a primary-replica Postgres, reads go to replicas. Support tickets: users see an old balance after a top-up for 1 to 3 seconds and sometimes can spend money twice. Log excerpt:

t0   POST /spend 80  balance read 100 (replica, lag 1.8s) -> ok
t0+1 POST /spend 80  balance read 100 (cache)             -> ok
final balance in primary: -60
replication_lag_seconds p99: 2.4
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and redesign, by data type.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Shortens the TTL.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the balance go negative? Which operations must be exact? Throughput of spends?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route balance reads and spends to the primary; disable balance caching.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Stale reads from replica lag and cache; read-modify-write without a lock or conditional update; the TTL is a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce with parallel spends; check lag metrics.
  5. Root cause: Same consistency level applied to money and profile data; the invariant (balance >= 0) is enforced on stale reads.
  6. Fix: Spend executes as one atomic statement on the primary: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 80, check rows affected; use a ledger table with an idempotency key. Cache and replicas only for display fields.
  7. Prevention: Property tests for invariants; alert on lag above a threshold and negative balances.
  8. Trade-offs: Primary reads cost capacity and latency; consistency model is a one-way door because code assumes it, so decide early. I would not use eventual consistency for money.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Primary becomes the bottleneck? -> Shard by wallet_id; each wallet's ops stay on one shard.
  • Show "recent" balance fast? -> Read-your-writes from primary for the owner for a short window.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Negative balances appeared only under promotions, when parallel spends spiked and lag exceeded two seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks TTL.
  • Hire: atomic conditional update, primary reads.
  • Strong hire: per-data-type consistency, ledger plus idempotency, gravity.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review of a launched media-upload service. Facts: a deploy to 100% of servers at once introduced a bug and caused 25 minutes of errors; nobody was alerted until customer support called (alerts existed only for CPU); an unauthenticated list endpoint exposed filenames of private uploads; the monthly cloud bill jumped 3x, 70% of it egress from serving originals directly from storage; schema change dropped a column during deploy.
questions.promptHtml: What operations, security and cost practices were missing, and what is your plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: A generic "add monitoring".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: SLOs? Who is on call? Data classification? Which cost line is largest?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add auth to the endpoint and rotate any exposed names; roll back; stop direct-original serving.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: No canary; no user-facing alerts; no authN/authZ review; no egress cost control; non-backward-compatible migration.
  4. How I'd verify: Review the deploy pipeline, alert rules, access logs, billing breakdown.
  5. Root cause: Operations treated as an afterthought.
  6. Fix: Alert: p99 above 500 ms for 5 minutes or error rate above 1% (golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation); 5% canary for 15 minutes, feature flags, automated rollback; authN/authZ on every endpoint, TLS, rate limit 100 req/min per user, PII encryption; serve via CDN with resized variants and move media older than 90 days to cold storage; expand-then-contract schema changes.
  7. Prevention: Launch checklist, security review, cost dashboards with budgets.
  8. Trade-offs: Canary slows releases by about 15 minutes, worth it; CDN adds cost but egress via CDN is usually cheaper per GB (verify for the provider); observability is cheap early and costly to retrofit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Canary shows no errors but a slow leak? -> Soak time and saturation metrics.
  • Dropped column needed rollback? -> That is why expand-contract: old code keeps working.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 3x bill was traced to a thumbnail endpoint serving full-size images; one resize step cut the line by roughly 60%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "add monitoring".
  • Hire: covers canary, alert metrics, auth, egress.
  • Strong hire: concrete thresholds, expand-contract, cost lever, gravity of retrofitting.

questions.contextHtml: A 12-engineer startup, 300 req/s, one Rails/Spring monolith with Postgres. A new architect proposes splitting into 20 microservices "to scale and move faster". Deploys currently take 40 minutes and the test suite takes 25. Two teams step on each other's code weekly. Infra budget is flat.
questions.promptHtml: Respond to the proposal. What do you recommend and what would change your mind?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either enthusiastic agreement or "never split".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the pain scaling or team coupling? Which modules change most? What is the deploy frequency target? Ops maturity (tracing, CI per service)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the actual pains first: speed up CI (parallelise tests), module boundaries.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The problems are deploy and test time and team contention, not throughput (300 req/s is tiny); microservices would add network hops (0.5 ms each), distributed transactions and operational load.
  4. How I'd verify: Measure change coupling in git history, deploy frequency, build timings.
  5. Root cause: An organisational and build problem presented as a scaling problem.
  6. Fix: Modular monolith with enforced boundaries, parallel CI, per-module ownership; extract one service where a clear trigger exists (independent scaling, different language, separate team).
  7. Prevention: Architecture decision records with explicit triggers.
  8. Trade-offs: Splitting is easy and merging back painful, a near one-way door; distributed transactions cost consistency. I would not refuse forever: extract the first service when a team or load boundary demands it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One module needs 50x the CPU? -> That is a valid extraction trigger.
  • Teams want independent deploys? -> Module-level feature flags first, then split.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company split into many services, then merged several back after tracing showed 60% of latency was cross-service hops.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees or refuses with no reasoning.
  • Hire: diagnoses actual pain, modular monolith.
  • Strong hire: triggers, gravity, cost of distribution, measured evidence.
